scenes.visual: THE WORLD, kept for both chapters (16:9, dark navy background). A Punnett grid of equal square BOXES drawn in thin WHITE lines; allele letters sit on the grid edges in WHITE; each box holds a LABEL chip coloured by phenotype: PURPLE for purple, RED for red, PINK for pink, pale GREY for white, YELLOW for yellow coat, near-BLACK with a white outline for black coat. A box whose label is 'dies' goes dark and its outline dashes. Ratios always appear on screen as text, never only spoken. For this chapter the grid is 4x4: rows are one parent's gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab), columns the other parent's. Title card 'Two Whites Make Purple' fades in over two white sweet-pea flowers.

scenes.tts: Can two white flowers have a purple child? Over a century ago, William Bateson, Edith Saunders and Reginald Punnett bred sweet peas to test Mendel's rules.
scenes.visual: Text tag 'Bateson, Saunders and Punnett, sweet peas, early 1900s'. Two sweet-pea plants with GREY-white flowers stand at left and right.
scenes.narration: Can two white flowers have a purple child? Over a century ago, William Bateson, Edith Saunders and Reginald Punnett bred sweet peas to test Mendel's rules.

scenes.tts: They crossed two white-flowered strains. Each strain bred true, giving only white flowers on its own. Yet every hybrid had purple flowers.
scenes.visual: A cross sign between the two white plants. Below, a row of hybrid plants grows; every flower opens PURPLE. Label 'every hybrid: purple'.
scenes.narration: They crossed two white-flowered strains. Each strain bred true, giving only white flowers on its own. Yet every hybrid had purple flowers.

scenes.tts: How can two white parents have a purple child?
scenes.visual: A question card over the purple hybrid: 'White x white gives purple. How?'
scenes.narration: How can two white parents have a purple child?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card stays; the two white parents and the purple hybrid hold still. A 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Here is the simplest model that fits. Suppose colour is made in two steps. Each step needs a working allele of a different gene.
scenes.visual: The card dissolves. A pathway draws left to right: a colourless starting molecule, arrow 'step 1 (gene A)', a colourless middle molecule, arrow 'step 2 (gene B)', a PURPLE pigment. A small tag reads 'model'.
scenes.narration: Here is the simplest model that fits. Suppose colour is made in two steps. Each step needs a working allele of a different gene.

scenes.tts: One white strain is broken at step one. The other is broken at step two. Neither can finish the pigment on its own.
scenes.visual: Two copies of the pathway, one under each white parent. Under the left parent, step 1's arrow carries a red X (aa). Under the right parent, step 2's arrow carries a red X (bb). Neither pathway reaches purple.
scenes.narration: One white strain is broken at step one. The other is broken at step two. Neither can finish the pigment on its own.

scenes.tts: The hybrid gets one working copy of each step, one from each parent. One copy of each is enough, so the hybrid makes colour. Each parent brings the step the other one lacks.
scenes.visual: The hybrid's pathway: step 1 lit by a working A from the right parent, step 2 lit by a working B from the left parent. The pigment fills PURPLE. Genotype label 'AaBb'.
scenes.narration: The hybrid gets one working copy of each step, one from each parent. One copy of each is enough, so the hybrid makes colour. Each parent brings the step the other one lacks.

scenes.tts: Next they let the hybrids pollinate themselves. Now the deal covers two genes. The genes are unlinked, so each hybrid makes four kinds of gamete, equally often.
scenes.visual: A hybrid plant with a self-pollination arrow. Four gamete tokens fan out from it: AB, Ab, aB, ab, each with '1/4' on screen.
scenes.narration: Next they let the hybrids pollinate themselves. Now the deal covers two genes. The genes are unlinked, so each hybrid makes four kinds of gamete, equally often.

scenes.tts: Pair them, and you get sixteen equally likely boxes. Nothing about the deal has changed.
scenes.visual: One parent's four gametes line the top of the 4x4 grid and the other parent's line the side; sixteen boxes fill with genotypes in small WHITE text. A padlock 'deal: fixed' settles on the grid lines.
scenes.narration: Pair them, and you get sixteen equally likely boxes. Nothing about the deal has changed.

scenes.tts: Light up every box with at least one working copy of both genes. Those boxes glow coloured.
scenes.visual: Boxes holding at least one A and at least one B light one by one with PURPLE chips tagged 'coloured'. A counter on screen reaches '9'.
scenes.narration: Light up every box with at least one working copy of both genes. Those boxes glow coloured.

scenes.tts: Each of the other boxes lacks a working copy for one step, or for both. Those boxes are white.
scenes.visual: The remaining boxes take pale GREY chips; each shows a small red X on the missing step (step 1, step 2, or both for aabb). Counter: '7'.
scenes.narration: Each of the other boxes lacks a working copy for one step, or for both. Those boxes are white.

scenes.tts: Their real flowers came close to this split of coloured to white. Their third report explained it as two genes that both need a dominant allele for colour. Some coloured plants were red, not purple; that took a further gene, which our model sets aside.
scenes.visual: Below the grid: '9 coloured : 7 white'. A text tag: 'Report III, 1906: two genes, each needs a dominant allele'. Then a small side note off the grid, not on any box: 'some coloured plants were red: a further gene, not in this model'. The nine coloured chips stay as they are.
scenes.narration: Their real flowers came close to this split of coloured to white. Their third report explained it as two genes that both need a dominant allele for colour. Some coloured plants were red, not purple; that took a further gene, which our model sets aside.

scenes.tts: They found the same in chickens. Two comb shapes crossed gave a third, and the next generation held four kinds of comb. One character can depend on two genes at once.
scenes.visual: The sweet-pea grid slides left and shrinks. At right, two chicken-head icons with different comb outlines; a cross sign; a third comb shape appears below. Then four comb outlines in a row with '9 : 3 : 3 : 1' under them. Text joins both panels: 'one character, two genes'.
scenes.narration: They found the same in chickens. Two comb shapes crossed gave a third, and the next generation held four kinds of comb. One character can depend on two genes at once.

scenes.tts: Notice what did not change. These are the ordinary sixteen boxes. The pathway never touched the deal. How the genes act only decided which boxes share a label.
scenes.visual: The colour chips lift slightly off the grid, showing the same sixteen genotype boxes underneath, then settle back. Text: 'same boxes, new labels'.
scenes.narration: Notice what did not change. These are the ordinary sixteen boxes. The pathway never touched the deal. How the genes act only decided which boxes share a label.

scenes.tts: Change how the genes act, and the same grid regroups. If a dominant allele at either gene is enough, only the box with none looks different.
scenes.visual: The chips shuffle to a new grouping: fifteen boxes share one chip, only aabb differs; on screen '15 : 1'. Then, silently, a second regrouping flashes: twelve, three and one, on screen '12 : 3 : 1'. The grid lines never move.
scenes.narration: Change how the genes act, and the same grid regroups. If a dominant allele at either gene is enough, only the box with none looks different.

scenes.tts: Bateson later used the word epistatic for a gene that hides the effect of another.
scenes.visual: Back to the 9:7 grid. The word 'epistatic' appears in WHITE, with a short gloss: 'a gene that hides the effect of another'.
scenes.narration: Bateson later used the word epistatic for a gene that hides the effect of another.

scenes.tts: Look at the second generation of a cross like this one. There, a ratio in sixteenths with fewer than four classes is a clue. Two unlinked genes may be acting on one trait.
scenes.visual: Three small ratio tags line up: '9 : 7', '15 : 1', '12 : 3 : 1', each with '/16' beneath. A bracket gathers them under the words 'clue: two unlinked genes, one trait'.
scenes.narration: Look at the second generation of a cross like this one. There, a ratio in sixteenths with fewer than four classes is a clue. Two unlinked genes may be acting on one trait.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed 4x4 grid, large white text, centred: 'Same sixteen boxes; how the genes act decides the labels.'
